title: Stateless services
summary: Why app servers must not depend on user data held in their own memory, and where that data goes instead.

blocks.p: A user logs in. The server that handled the login stores the user's session in its own memory and sends back a cookie with the session's ID. The next request goes through the load balancer and lands on a different server.
That server has never heard of the session. To it, the user is logged out. Adding servers made the app break.

A **stateless** server keeps nothing between requests that another server would need. Each request carries what is needed to handle it, or the server fetches it from a shared place. Then any server can handle any request.

blocks.caption: Three ways to handle a login across two servers. Only the shared session store survives both a different server and a failed one.

blocks.p: The session lives on server 1. When the load balancer sends the next request to server 2, the session isn't there and the request fails.

The load balancer can remember which server each user went to, usually with a cookie, and keep sending them there. This works until server 1 fails or is replaced. Then its sessions are gone, and its users are logged out.

Every server writes sessions to a shared store, such as a database or an in-memory key-value store. Any server can read any session, so the load balancer can send each request anywhere, and losing a server loses no sessions.

blocks.h3: Or put the state in the request

blocks.p: Another option is to put the session data itself in a token that the client sends with every request. The server signs the token so it can detect changes. A **JSON Web Token**, defined in [RFC 7519](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7519), is a common format. A signed token is readable by the client, so keep secrets out of it. It also stays valid until it expires, so logging a user out early needs extra work.

list: **The Twelve-Factor App says it plainly.** Its [processes rule](https://12factor.net/processes) says processes are stateless and share nothing, and calls sticky sessions a violation of that rule.

**Load balancers offer stickiness anyway.** [AWS Application Load Balancer](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elasticloadbalancing/latest/application/sticky-sessions.html) can bind a user's session to a target with a cookie. It is useful for old applications that can't move their state.
**Uploads and files are state too.** A file written to one server's local disk is missing on the others. Put files in object storage, covered in the object storage lesson.
**Stateless doesn't mean no state.** The state still exists. It moves to a database, a cache or the client, where it can be shared and kept safe.
A stateless server keeps nothing between requests that another server would need.
Sessions in server memory break as soon as there is a second server.
Sticky sessions hide the problem until a server fails.
Move state to a shared store, or into a signed token the client sends back.
